title: Mohnish Pabrai Q&A at Harvard Business School Investment Conference - April 4, 2022
summary: In conversation with HBS professor Nori Gerardo Lietz, Pabrai argues that Ben Graham 'led him astray' by selling at intrinsic value and explains his recent shift to holding great compounders above intrinsic value. He uses Reysas in Turkey as a real-world case of micro trumping macro (bought a third of the company for $7 million against $800 million of liquidation value), discusses his 170-question checklist built from great investors' mistakes, the Seritage exit, shameless cloning, and why the job is to read and think rather than act.

ideas.idea: Fiat Chrysler in 2012 was a spectacular investment despite his lifelong hatred of the auto industry: about $140 billion of revenue for a $5 billion market cap.
ideas.detail: The umbrella included Ferrari, Maserati, Alfa Romeo, Jeep and Ram; Ferrari alone is now worth about $60 billion. He invested even with unions and competitive issues because all union contracts had been redone and Detroit had become a great place to make cars.

ideas.idea: Ben Graham's three cornerstones remain the foundation: stocks are fractional ownership of a business, insist on a margin of safety, and make Mr. Market work for you.
ideas.detail: Graham's portfolio was clobbered from 1929 to 1938, which produced Security Analysis and the net-net approach of paying two-thirds of net current assets; those bargains are very hard to find today.

ideas.idea: Ben Graham led him astray for most of his career: the mistake was treating intrinsic value as a red line for selling, when the most money is made by holding businesses with long growth runways well above intrinsic value.
ideas.detail: A Graham investor in Walmart in the 1970s would have exited at 40-50x earnings and missed the forest for the trees. He figured this out only two or three years ago and reckons he has '22 years of runway left' to make amends.

ideas.idea: Value and growth are two sides of one coin; all intelligent investing is value investing, and the only thing that changed in his framework is holding above perceived intrinsic value.
ideas.detail: Two $1 billion businesses, one paying $100 million flat for 50 years and one growing 10% for 25-30 years, both have a discountable value per John Burr Williams; you invest where the gap between price and value is greatest. The difficulty is that future cash flows are unknowable in most cases and only boundable in a sliver.

ideas.idea: Reysas in 2019 was a once-in-a-lifetime anomaly: a $20 million market cap against $800 million of liquidation value, so he bought a third of the company for $7 million without needing to estimate future cash flows.
ideas.detail: 83 warehouses totaling 12 million square feet, 99% leased on 10-year inflation-indexed leases to Ikea, Carrefour and Amazon, worth about $1 billion less $200 million of debt. The stock is up 5-6x in dollars since and still sits at about 10 cents on the dollar; the company is also Turkey's largest freight rail operator, truck fleet, forklift renter and vehicle inspection station owner.

ideas.idea: He would not sell a single Reysas share even if the market valued it at his optimistic $1.5 billion intrinsic value, because the 37-year-old son running it is an exceptional capital allocator, better than the father.
ideas.detail: Liquidation value is now at least $1 billion and intrinsic value perhaps $1.5 billion once the family's capital allocation is included; that is what holding above intrinsic value means in practice.

ideas.idea: Micro trumps macro: with 50% real inflation in Turkey (the official 25% is fiction), he only buys businesses that benefit from or are immune to the chaos.
ideas.detail: The lira went from 5 to nearly 15 per dollar since 2019 (a 70% decline), yet Reysas is up 18x in lira and 6x in dollars. Its CapEx was done in yesterday's lira, leases reset at least at the 25% official rate and go to market after 10 years, and its little debt is at 14%; a juice exporter with 98% euro revenue and lira costs also sees rising euro profits. Most Turkish businesses get hurt and he has no interest in them.

ideas.idea: Turkey is the cheapest market in the world because everyone has exited, and spending time on 50 Turkish companies is more worthwhile than anything in the US.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: He is 'most orgasmic' about Turkey; he has only one US holding (bought 2018) plus a 2020 purchase already sold, because he cannot find obvious investments in the US that his 'little brain' can understand.

ideas.idea: His brain does not try to figure out the economy; it starts with a single business and asks what it looks like 5, 10 or 15 years out, which is only possible for a small sliver of businesses.
ideas.detail: Within his circle he expects a 50-60% success rate, which with 'two-by-four' no-brainers produces great results; he does not waste time on questions that full-time macro experts cannot answer.

ideas.idea: You make money by waiting, not by buying or selling; when things do not make sense there is no compulsion to act and it is fine to pass on 99%.
ideas.detail: In a typical year he finds zero to three things to buy and zero to three to sell. The job description is to read and think, not to act; investors who expect weekly activity invested with the wrong guy.

ideas.idea: He is unconcerned about assets under management or investors leaving; if all outside money left he would manage his own and make Reysas half the portfolio.
ideas.detail: Much of his reading is unrelated to investments, e.g. 'The CEO Factory' about Hindustan Unilever, which has compounded at 16% a year for 65 years.

ideas.idea: His checklist, built about 14 years ago from great investors' losing bets (via 13F filings), shows the biggest causes of failure are leverage, misjudged moats and management or ownership issues, all visible beforehand.
ideas.detail: For each loss he asked why it failed and whether the data was visible before the investment, e.g. Buffett's US Air, where Southwest's low-cost attack on the Pittsburgh hub was a misread moat. The list now has about 170 questions and typically surfaces 7-10 unknowns that force another month or two of research before a go/no-go decision, since every business has issues.

ideas.idea: He exited Seritage after admitting he underestimated how hard redeveloping properties across a hundred different municipalities would be; the real mistake was opportunity cost in Q2 2020.
ideas.detail: Bought at $6-9 after it fell from $30+ pre-pandemic, sold for a 20-40% gain, but many other cheap companies were available then. Templeton said the best analysts are right two out of three times, and realistically it is about half; being honest with yourself and taking chips off the table when a thesis is flawed is essential.

ideas.idea: Be a shameless cloner: nobody is smart enough to invent everything, so ride on the shoulders of Graham, Buffett and especially Munger.
ideas.detail: Microsoft's research labs spent tens of billions for almost nothing while Word came from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus 1-2-3, Teams from Zoom and Edge from Chrome; Burger King's two guys follow McDonald's site selection; the only airlines that thrived (e.g. Ryanair) cloned Southwest. Something in the human psyche looks down on cloning, which is why it gives a massive edge.

ideas.idea: Idea generation should start from lists that have already passed through a good brain: a Graham investor's Turkish portfolio, Dataroma, or Bill Ackman's 13F.
ideas.detail: In Turkey he visited only the companies his friend had already put money behind rather than a hundred at random; Ackman's picks have perhaps a 50% batting average, still better than throwing darts.

ideas.idea: The bottom of the market is continuously cleared of great talent as successful managers outgrow small bets, so emerging managers always have nooks and crannies available.
ideas.detail: Per Joel Greenblatt, a $5 million manager can make $100,000-$500,000 bets that move the needle; once $5 million becomes $500 million they must leave the bottom. Managers worth studying include Josh Tarasoff and Andrew Wilkinson of Tiny Capital.

ideas.idea: He bought a Ferrari 488 Spider in 2018 because he made so much money on the stock, and it never went down in price during his ownership; Ferrari never discounts.
ideas.detail: Ferrari could help with delivery (normally a 2-3 year wait) but not price. After moving to Austin he swapped it for a Ram Longhorn at a quarter the price and stays loyal to the Chrysler brands.
